title: Durable monetization: How four AI founders solved the pricing puzzle
gist: Bessemer argues that durable AI pricing ties revenue to something a customer can independently verify on their own dashboard, and that hard, closed-loop ROI commands premium pricing while copilot-style soft ROI compresses it. Four portfolio founders (Recall.ai, Strella, Graph AI, Ada) each landed on a different model — usage, seat, outcome, hybrid — because customer value, fungibility and delivery economics interact differently in each business, and 2026 is the first year most AI contracts get re-underwritten at renewal against delivered outcomes.

themes.theme: The renewal test: 2026 re-underwriting of AI contracts

insights.claim: 2026 is the first year most AI companies will face contract renewal at scale, and many deals signed during the 2025 adoption rush were not structured to survive it.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Treat 2026 net revenue retention as the first honest read on AI software durability; NRR compression in AI vendors is a timing signal, not necessarily a demand signal.
insights.quote: 2026 is the first year that most AI companies will face renewal at scale, and many contracts signed during 2025's adoption rush weren't built for this moment.
insights.locator: The renewal test: What separates pricing that holds

insights.claim: Enterprise buyers bought AI on potential with minimal price scrutiny in initial purchase cycles and are now re-underwriting renewals against delivered outcomes rather than original promise.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Vendors without instrumented, customer-visible outcome data face repricing at renewal — ask portfolio companies what evidence a buyer can pull independently.
insights.quote: Buyers who signed on potential are now renewing on proof.
insights.locator: Most companies spent initial purchase cycles in adoption mode

insights.claim: Durable AI pricing units share one property: the customer can independently verify the metered quantity on their own dashboard — infrastructure consumed, seats activated, workflow automated, conversations resolved, or tasks completed.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Use 'can the buyer verify this number without the vendor' as a fast diligence filter on AI revenue quality.
insights.quote: A customer who can point to their own dashboard and see the value delivered doesn't need to take the vendor's word for it at contract time.
insights.locator: None of these companies are pricing on a promise.

themes.theme: Three drivers of AI pricing power

insights.claim: Bessemer partner Adam Fisher frames AI pricing power as the interaction of exactly three variables: customer value created, fungibility (how easily the product can be replaced), and delivery economics or COGS.
insights.speaker: Adam Fisher
insights.so_what: A reusable three-axis scorecard for underwriting whether an AI company can hold price through a downturn or a renewal cycle.
insights.locator: Three drivers of pricing power for AI products

insights.claim: Unlike traditional SaaS where serving one more customer costs virtually nothing, AI products incur real per-query costs, and some also carry heavy human services, implementation, or domain-expert delivery costs that must be designed around before choosing a pricing model.
insights.speaker: Adam Fisher
insights.so_what: Gross margin structure, not ARR growth, is the differentiator between AI businesses that scale profitably and those that do not.
insights.quote: Unlike traditional SaaS, where the cost of serving one more customer is virtually zero, AI products incur real costs with every query.
insights.locator: 3. Delivery economics (i.e. cost of goods sold or COGS)

insights.claim: Defensibility that comes from proprietary data, domain expertise, model performance, workflow design, or deep integration into customer systems translates directly into pricing power, especially when replacing the product with human labor is impractical.
insights.speaker: Adam Fisher
insights.so_what: Where the only substitute is rehiring headcount, price ceilings are set by labor cost, not by competing software.
insights.locator: 2. Fungibility

insights.claim: There is no single winning formula for AI pricing; a bespoke approach is the right entry point, and the operative question is how a business manufactures pricing power given its specific industry, ICP, and go-to-market motion.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Benchmarking an AI company's pricing model against peers is misleading; evaluate fit to its own value, defensibility and COGS instead.
insights.quote: How does a business manufacture pricing power given its unique variables (industry, ICP, GTM motion)?
insights.locator: A bespoke approach is often the right entry point

themes.theme: Proof of impact: hard ROI vs soft ROI

insights.claim: Two AI products can create identical customer value yet command entirely different prices, because the one that can prove it closed the loop has pricing power and the one that can only claim it helped does not.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Attribution infrastructure is itself a monetizable moat; underwrite proof mechanics, not just model quality.
insights.quote: Two products can create identical customer value and still command entirely different prices if one can prove it closed the loop and the other can only claim it helped.
insights.locator: The power of monetizing proof

insights.claim: Copilot products generate soft ROI that compresses willingness to pay because buyers ask whether the outcome would have happened anyway, while agentic products that complete the workflow end-to-end produce results that are measurable, attributable, and much harder to negotiate down.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Structurally favor end-to-end agentic vendors over assistive copilots when pricing durability is the question.
insights.quote: soft ROI compresses willingness to pay because customers wonder, "Would this outcome have happened anyway?"
insights.locator: For example, a copilot that surfaces the right answer

insights.claim: Bessemer cites Sweep's workflow completion and Sett.ai's closed-loop delivery as hard-ROI products that renew on the strength of their own evidence, while sophisticated products still in soft-ROI territory face a prove-value-or-reprice conversation.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Named examples of the hard-ROI archetype worth tracking as renewal-cycle proof points.
insights.locator: Products built on hard ROI, such as Sweep's workflow completion

insights.claim: Service-replacement AI plays by a different rule than efficiency or revenue-uplift products: it is sold on total cost of ownership, and winners force an honest TCO comparison rather than letting buyers compare sticker price to sticker price.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Enterprises routinely undercount legacy costs — founders who make that gap visible capture the replacement budget, a repeatable GTM tell.
insights.quote: Enterprises routinely undercount what their legacy approach actually costs; founders who can make that gap visible are the ones who capture the replacement budget.
insights.locator: However, service replacement plays by a different rule entirely.

insights.claim: Across the past year AI companies have experimented with usage-, workflow-, outcome-, and hybrid pricing, and outcome pricing generates the most revenue momentum — but the cost-benefit tradeoff depends entirely on which customers are served.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Outcome pricing is a momentum accelerant, not a universal answer; check ICP fit before treating it as a positive signal.
insights.quote: Increasingly, businesses gain the most revenue momentum by pricing on outcomes, but the cost-benefit tradeoff depends entirely on the ideal customers they serve.
insights.locator: Over the past year, AI companies have experimented

themes.theme: Recall.ai: usage pricing that aligns value with COGS

insights.claim: Recall.ai charges for meeting-data infrastructure on a usage basis so that the bill rises only when a customer's own product succeeds and processes more conversation data, creating what CEO David Gu calls an 'alignment of success'.
insights.speaker: David Gu
insights.so_what: Infra vendors whose revenue is a derivative of customer success have embedded expansion without a sales motion — high-quality net revenue retention.
insights.quote: if your product becomes very successful and you’re now processing a lot of data, Recall.ai is going to cost more
insights.locator: As co-founder and CEO David Gu explains

insights.claim: Recall.ai's usage model exists partly because infrastructure providers incur real costs as customers consume more resources, so consumption pricing keeps COGS scaling in lockstep with revenue rather than decoupling them.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Consumption pricing at infra layers is a margin-protection mechanism, not just a GTM preference.
insights.locator: This approach also reflects Recall.ai's delivery economics.

insights.claim: Usage-based pricing has low buyer friction for developer infrastructure because customers already procure cloud, APIs, and AI models on consumption terms, avoiding seat-license friction and complex pricing tiers.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Procurement familiarity is an underrated driver of pricing model adoption — buyers accept the metering they already run.
insights.locator: That alignment extends beyond economics.

insights.claim: Recall.ai's defensibility rests on specialized meeting-capture infrastructure — audio, video, transcripts, and metadata — that developers cannot easily replicate themselves, which is what lets it monetize consumption at all.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Low fungibility is the precondition for usage pricing; commoditized infra gets priced to marginal cost instead.
insights.locator: Recall.ai neatly illustrates the interaction

themes.theme: Strella: optimize for adoption when AI is not the dominant cost

insights.claim: Strella deliberately chose seat-based pricing over per-interview or per-project pricing for its AI qualitative research platform, prioritizing product adoption over short-term value capture.
insights.speaker: Lydia Hylton
insights.so_what: A counterexample to the outcome-pricing consensus: adoption velocity can be worth more than per-unit capture in a usage-elastic category.
insights.quote: We wanted to remove every barrier to running a Strella interview that you possibly could have
insights.locator: 2. Strella: Remove barriers to adoption before optimizing for revenue

insights.claim: Per-interview or per-project pricing would force research teams to seek budget approval every time they ran a study, slowing usage and deterring customers, whereas a seat model lets customers negotiate spend once and then run research freely.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Approval friction per transaction is a hidden growth tax — watch for it wherever usage pricing meets discretionary budgets.
insights.locator: Charging per interview or project would require teams

insights.claim: Strella's cost per AI-moderated interview is trivial next to the cost of paying the human research participant, so AI inference was never the dominant cost driver and the company was not forced into usage pricing to protect margins.
insights.speaker: Lydia Hylton
insights.so_what: When AI cost is small relative to the labor displaced, founders gain pricing flexibility rather than pricing pressure — a screen for which AI categories can afford seat pricing.
insights.quote: cost per interview pales in comparison to the cost of paying the person for their time who's participating in the interview.
insights.locator: Critically, Strella's delivery economics gave the team flexibility.

insights.claim: Strella's differentiation is its research-specific product and workflow — an AI moderator built to conduct natural, adaptive interviews — not the underlying frontier model, which the company treats as increasingly commoditized.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Application-layer moats must sit above the model; commoditized model access means workflow IP carries the defensibility.
insights.quote: access to frontier models is increasingly commoditized
insights.locator: The reason this pricing model works

insights.claim: Strella treats revenue predictability as an explicit asset of the seat-based model, with CEO Lydia Hylton stating that predictable revenue is worth more than unpredictable revenue.
insights.speaker: Lydia Hylton
insights.so_what: Revenue-quality multiple expansion argument: subscription predictability can outweigh higher but volatile usage revenue at exit.
insights.quote: Predictable revenue is worth more than unpredictable revenue.
insights.locator: Ultimately, Strella optimized pricing for long-term growth

themes.theme: Graph AI: price against the labor category, not the software category

insights.claim: Graph AI CEO Raghavendra Parvataraju says pharmacovigilance customers currently send 75% of their spend to human labor and only 25% to software, and Graph AI is inverting that ratio so 75% of the heavy lifting is handled by software with 25% requiring human oversight.
insights.speaker: Raghavendra Parvataraju
insights.so_what: Quantifies the addressable pool for services-replacement AI in regulated life sciences: the labor 75%, not the software 25%.
insights.quote: Today, customers are forced into a model where 75% of their spend goes toward human labor and only 25% toward the software that's supposed to help them. We're inverting that ratio.
insights.locator: "A lot of these services are delivered by people

insights.claim: Graph AI benchmarks its price against the combined cost of the software plus the human review it replaces rather than against other pharmacovigilance platforms, on the principle that the unit of pricing should follow the unit of value created.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Vendors anchored to labor budgets have far higher price ceilings than those anchored to software seat comps — a key valuation input for services-replacement AI.
insights.quote: it prices the value it creates, not simply the technology it sells.
insights.locator: Graph AI uses an outcome-based model.

insights.claim: Graph AI claims 90%+ efficiency gains and 65% cost savings on automated pharmacovigilance workflows, backed by deep life sciences expertise and regulatory-grade AI that is difficult to replicate.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Concrete efficiency benchmark for what regulated-workflow automation can deliver, useful for sizing comparable claims elsewhere.
insights.quote: Automates pharmacovigilance workflows with 90%+ efficiency gains and 65% cost savings
insights.locator: 3. Graph AI: Price against the labor you're replacing

insights.claim: Legacy pharmacovigilance labor is barbell-shaped — a large low-cost-per-head front end of sourcing, intake, data entry and triage staffed by pharmacology and BPO resources, plus a small high-cost back end of quality and medical reviewers — and Graph AI automates the front end outright while making reviewers spend expertise on judgment rather than preparation.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: The automate-the-volume-tier, augment-the-expert-tier pattern is a transferable template for attacking any services-heavy regulated workflow.
insights.locator: That inversion reflects the shape of the labor being replaced.

insights.claim: Graph AI front-loads its heaviest processing early in a case's lifecycle, so incremental cost falls as the case progresses and the platform becomes more profitable per case at volume rather than carrying flat costs throughout.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: A specific mechanism for margin expansion with scale in agentic workflow products — ask whether compute is front-loaded or amortized flat.
insights.locator: Graph AI automates the high-volume front end outright

insights.claim: Graph AI ties each new product module to a new pricing tier, so as automation extends from individual safety case processing to report generation and eventually larger portions of review, each capability creates additional value that justifies the next price step.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: A pricing architecture where roadmap execution mechanically converts into price increases — durable ACV expansion without new logos.
insights.locator: Rather than anchoring prices to software seats or licenses

insights.claim: Per-case pricing is easier for pharmacovigilance customers to budget than seat licensing because safety case volumes are relatively stable and forecastable, aligning the commercial model with how customers plan spend.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Usage pricing is buyer-friendly only where volume is predictable; volatile-volume categories will resist it.
insights.locator: The model also offers customers predictability.

themes.theme: Ada: buyer preference overrides value-optimal pricing

insights.claim: Ada originally charged per resolved conversation because outcome pricing lowered adoption barriers for early enterprise adopters testing AI in production, but CEO Mike Murchison says there were a lot of challenges with outcome-based pricing as the market matured.
insights.speaker: Mike Murchison
insights.so_what: A live counterweight to the outcome-pricing hype: the model's appeal was a function of the experimentation phase, not a permanent equilibrium.
insights.quote: There were a lot of challenges with outcome-based pricing
insights.locator: But as the market evolved, so did customers’ buying preferences.

insights.claim: As Ada became embedded in core business operations rather than an experiment, enterprise customers shifted from paying for measurable outcomes to preferring predictable annual budgets and multi-year contracts, and Ada changed its model to match.
insights.speaker: Mike Murchison
insights.so_what: Expect an industry-wide drift from outcome billing back toward committed contracts as AI moves from pilot to infrastructure — a leading indicator of category maturity.
insights.locator: However, as the promise of AI became more fully realized

insights.claim: Ada's current hybrid model has three components — a platform fee for technology access, a usage fee based on conversation volume purchased upfront, and an implementation fee for integrating AI agents into customers' back-office systems.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: A concrete packaging template: separate variable compute from fixed integration cost instead of burying both in one resolution fee.
insights.locator: Its pricing consists of three components

insights.claim: Ada's delivery economics work because it splits variable, volume-scaled compute costs from fixed, upfront integration costs rather than pricing both as a single resolution fee.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Bundling implementation into per-outcome pricing hides a fixed cost inside a variable line — a structural margin risk to check in AI agent companies.
insights.locator: 4. Ada: The best pricing model is the one that matches how customers buy

insights.claim: Mike Murchison argues the business case is identical whether the customer pays for a resolution or a conversation, because it is still rooted in an expected resolution rate plus incremental improvement in customer experience quality — the value story stayed constant while the packaging changed.
insights.speaker: Mike Murchison
insights.so_what: Pricing model changes are not always value-story changes; distinguish repackaging from real deterioration when a vendor moves off outcome pricing.
insights.quote: Whether or not the customer is paying directly for a resolution or a conversation, the business case is the same.
insights.locator: As Mike puts it

insights.claim: Bessemer's lesson from Ada is that customer value, defensibility and delivery economics determine which pricing models are viable but not which one customers will actually prefer, so the commercial model must align with enterprise procurement behavior even when a different model captures more value.
insights.speaker: Christine Deakers
insights.so_what: Adds a fourth, demand-side constraint to the three-driver framework: procurement preference can veto the theoretically optimal model.
